I

—

The

Attorney-General's

discretion

Historically,

the

Attorney-General

has

the

discretionary

power

to

prosecute

or

not

to

prosecute

a

law-breaker

and

to

stay

or

withdraw

proceedings

already

instituted.

He

only

answers

to

Parliament

for

his

actions.

The

courts

have

traditionally

refused

to

review

the

appropriateness

of

his

decisions

for

two

principle

reasons:

the

separation

of

powers,

and

a

concern

not

to

affect

the

efficacy

of

the

accusatory

system.

If

it

were

possible

to

scrutinize

the

Attorney-General's

reasons

for

not

laying

charges,

logic

would

justify

the

same

exercise

when

he

did

lay

charges.

Trial

within

a

reasonable

delay

would

therefore

become

utopie

because

the

courts

would

be

flooded

with

applications

for

review.

This

undoubtedly

explains

the

name

of

this

position

—

the

flood-gate

principle.

These

observations

have

been

abundantly

commented

on

in

doctrinal

works,

notably

in

Edwards,

in

(New

20ff.

For

centuries,

the

Attorney-General's

primary

responsibility

was

maintaining

the

sovereign's

interests

in

the

royal

courts,

resulting

in

his

status

as

principal

law

officer

of

the

Crown

and

as

head

of

the

bar.

With

the

supremacy

of

Parliament,

his

functions

expanded

greatly,

and

he

became,

not

only

advisor

to

government

and

member

of

Parliament,

but

in

a

number

of

respects

the

representative

of

the

public

interest.

Along

with

the

exalted

status

of

his

office

come

high

expectations

as

to

the

Attorney-General's

performance

of

his

functions.

A

large

measure

of

constitu

tional

trust

is

reposed

within

him,

and

he

bears

a

heavy

obligation

to

conduct

himself

with

dignity

and

fairness.

In

many

situations,

he

is

described

as

acting

either

judicially

or

quasi-judicially.

When

exercising

his

"grave"

discretion

in

prosecutorial

matters,

he

must

take

into

account

not

only

the

position

of

the

individual,

but

what

the

public

interest

demands.

In

doing

so,

he

must

stand

alone,

acting

independently

of

political

or

other

external

influences.

He

is

to

be

neither

instructed

or

restrained,

save

by

his

final

accountability

to

Parliament.

II

The

ministerial

decisions

Notwithstanding

traditional

attitude

of

the

discretionary

of

Attorney-General

in

criminal

matters,

counsel

Brabant

and

Girouard

strongly

argue

that

the

Attorney-General

cannot

refuse

to

apply

the

law.

He

can

also

not

discriminate

in

prosecutorial

power.
